newsitem.title: USA: Senators seek whether Pentagon in Gulf War cover up.
newsitem.headline: Senators seek whether Pentagon in Gulf War cover up.

text.p: Senate committee leaders vowed on Thursday to find out whether the Pentagon tried to cover up Gulf War troops' possible war gas exposure and one said retired Gen. Norman Schwarzkopf had logs that could help.

"We are concerned as to what the Department of Defence did," Senate Veterans Committee Chairman Arlen Specter said at a hearing on Gulf War illnesses. "Was it indifference? Was it carelessness? Was it recklessness? Was it a cover up? And that we intend to pursue in depth."

The committee's senior Democrat, Sen. Jay Rockefeller of West Virginia, said he personally believed someone deliberately got rid of official military logs for the eight days in March 1991 when U.S. troops unknowingly blew up chemical weapons in an Iraqi arms dump, exposing up to 20,000 troops to the war gas. But he said retired Gulf War commander Schwarzkopf had his own personal logs of what happened during that period and had not made them public.

"I happen to think those eight days (of official logs) were disposed of for ill purposes," Rockefeller said. "... I have no proof of that. That's my view. But certainly those eight days are going to be covered by the (Schwarzkopf) log."

Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon lashed out at the senators' suggestions both of a Pentagon coverup and of the possibility that the Schwarzkopf logs might show whether the military knew in 1991 of troops' possible gas war exposure.
"I think this is a wild goose chase, frankly, on your part and also on the parts of Senator Rockefeller and Senator Specter," Bacon told reporters in response to questions about the Schwarzkopf logs.

He said Schwarzkopf has said repeatedly that he had no evidence of any chemical exposure to U.S. troops in the Gulf, and said a presidential panel reported this week that it had found no evidence of a Gulf illness cover-up.

Bacon said that although Schwarzkopf had received a ruling from government lawyers that the logs were his personal property, he offered on Dec. 23 to allow Pentagon investigators to come to his home in Tampa to examine them.

Bacon said the department would send someone to look at the retired commander's complete logs. Defence officials said Schwarzkopf had also offered to allow representatives from both Rockefeller's and Specter's offices to see the logs.
An official at the Pentagon said earlier this week that it hoped to report shortly on its inquiry into what happened to the eight days of March 1991 logs that were missing.

Those logs, kept by Schwarzkopf's command headquarters in Riyadh in Saudi Arabia, covered both March 4 and March 10, 1991, dates that U.S. troops blew up the Iraqi arms dump which investigators now say contained sarin and mustard gas weapons.
